verses.zh: 以色列人又行耶和华眼中看为恶的事，耶和华就把他们交在米甸人手里七年。
verses.en: The Israelites did evil in the Lord’s sight,[NOTE:1] so the Lord turned them over to[NOTE:2] Midian for seven years.
notes: Heb “in the eyes of.”
Heb “gave them into the hand of.”
verses.commentary:
6:1 "the Lord gave them into the hands of Midian" Midian is a southern nomadic
tribe south of Edom. The people are relatives of the Hebrews through Keturah (cf. Gen. 25:1). They are linked to the Kenites
(cf. Num. 10:29; Jdgs. 1:16). Moses' father-in-law was a priest of this tribe.

▣ "into the hands" This is a Semitic idiom for power (cf. Jdgs. 6:9). The NASB translates "hand" in 6:2 as "power."

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

verses.zh: 米甸人压制以色列人；以色列人因为米甸人，就在山中挖穴、挖洞、建造营寨。
verses.en: The Midianites[NOTE:1] overwhelmed Israel.[NOTE:2] Because of Midian the Israelites made shelters[NOTE:3] for themselves in the hills, caves, and strongholds.
notes: Heb “the hand of Midian.”
Heb “The hand of Midian was strong against Israel.”
Or possibly “secret storage places.” The Hebrew word occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible.
verses.commentary:
6:2 "the sons of Israel made for themselves the dens which were in the mountains and the caves and the strongholds"
The Israelites had to (1) live in hide-aways (Josephus, Antiq. 5.6.1) or (2) hide their food in the mountains because
of the pressure of the Midianites in the valleys.

verses.zh: 以色列人每逢撒种之后，米甸人、亚玛力人，和东方人都上来攻打他们，
verses.en: Whenever the Israelites planted their crops,[NOTE:1] the Midianites, Amalekites, and the people from the east would attack them.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Whenever Israel sowed seed.”
Heb “Midian, Amalek, and the sons of the east would go up, they would go up against him.” The translation assumes that וְעָלוּ (veʿalu) is dittographic (note the following עָלָיו, ʿalayv).
verses.commentary:
6:3 "that the Midianites would come up with the Amalekites and the sons of the east" This referred to three different
groups (cf. Jdgs. 6:33).

- the Midianites mentioned in Jdgs. 6:1

- the Amalekites mentioned in Jdgs. 3:13, who were also related to the Hebrews through Esau (cf. Gen. 36:12), but whose
name became a synonym of treachery and evil because of the way they treated the people of God during the exodus period

- the term "the sons of the east," which refers to a third group, possibly a non-Semitic group (cf. Gen. 29:1), northeast of
Canaan (cf. Jdgs. 6:3, 33; 7:12; 8:10; 1 Kgs. 4:30; Job 1:3; Isa. 11:14; Jer. 49:28; Ezek. 25:4,10)

Josephus' Antiq. 5.6.1 calls these three groups, "the Midianites called the Amalekites and Arabians."

6:4, 5 These non-Israelite, nomadic invaders apparently swarmed into the land during the time of harvest and stole
the annual crop along with the livestock of the Israelites.

verses.zh: 对着他们安营，毁坏土产，直到迦萨，没有给以色列人留下食物，牛、羊、驴也没有留下；
verses.en: They invaded the land[NOTE:1] and devoured[NOTE:2] its crops[NOTE:3] all the way to Gaza. They left nothing for the Israelites to eat,[NOTE:4] and they took away[NOTE:5] the sheep, oxen, and donkeys.
notes: Heb “They encamped against them.”
Heb “destroyed.”
Heb “the crops of the land.”
Heb “They left no sustenance in Israel.”
The words “they took away” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
verses.commentary:
6:4 "destroy the produce of the earth" Because of Jdgs. 6:5 the New Oxford Annotated Bible, p. 308, suggests
this refers to taxation. The JPSOA has a footnote that suggests it means "grazed" and involves the over-grazing of the
invaders' herds.

However, to me, Jdgs. 6:4-5 implies stealing Israel's crops and herds.

verses.zh: 因为那些人带着牲畜帐棚来，像蝗虫那样多，人和骆驼无数，都进入国内，毁坏全地。
verses.en: When they invaded[NOTE:1] with their cattle and tents, they were as thick[NOTE:2] as locusts. Neither they nor their camels could be counted.[NOTE:3] They came to devour[NOTE:4] the land.
notes: Heb “came up.”
Heb “numerous.”
Heb “To them and to their camels there was no number.”
Heb “destroy.” The translation “devour” carries through the imagery of a locust plague earlier in this verse.
verses.commentary:
6:5 "their camels were innumerable" This is the first mention of domesticated camels. They were domesticated
around the 12th century B.C. This would mean that these groups had the most advanced form of desert travel, military
technology, and also their numbers were very large.

▣ "like locust" A locust plague is used in Joel as a metaphor of military invasion (cf. Jdgs. 7:12; also note
Isa. 33:4; Jer. 46:23; 51:14, 27; Amos 4:9-10).

Locusts were one of YHWH's plagues on Egypt (cf. Exodus 10; Ps. 78:46; 105:34). They also formed
part of the "cursing" section of Deut. 28:38, 42.

There are several words in Hebrew which refer to locusts. This shows their prominence in the ANE. It is
uncertain if the words refer to

- stages of the locust's life

- different kinds of locusts

verses.zh: 以色列人因米甸人的缘故，极其穷乏，就呼求耶和华。
verses.en: Israel was so severely weakened by Midian that the Israelites cried out to the Lord for help.
verses.commentary:
6:6 "cried to the Lord" This is part of a recurrent cycle of sin, judgment, and repentance
which characterizes the book of Judges (cf. Jdgs. 3:9, 15; 6:6, 7; 10:10, 14).

verses.zh: 以色列人因米甸人的缘故，呼求耶和华，
verses.en: When the Israelites cried out to the Lord for help because of Midian,

verses.zh: 耶和华就差遣先知到以色列人那里，对他们说：「耶和华―以色列的　神如此说：『我曾领你们从埃及上来，出了为奴之家，
verses.en: the Lord sent a prophet[NOTE:1] to the Israelites. He said to them, “This is what the Lord God of Israel has said: ‘I brought you up from Egypt[NOTE:2] and took you out of that place of slavery.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “a man, a prophet.” Hebrew idiom sometimes puts a generic term before a more specific designation.

Some ancient witnesses read “from the land of Egypt.” מֵאֶרֶץ (meʾerets, “from the land [of]”) could have been accidentally omitted by homoioarcton (note the following מִמִּצְרַיִם [mimmitsrayim, “from Egypt”]).
Heb “of the house of slavery.”
verses.commentary:
6:8 "the Lord sent a prophet to the sons of Israel" This is an unnamed prophet. He
repeats the exodus covenant promises of God's trustworthiness as demonstrated in the deliverance from Egypt. Some
scholars try to interpret this as "the angel/messenger of the Lord," but this does not fit Jdgs. 6:21-24.

verses.zh: 救你们脱离埃及人的手，并脱离一切欺压你们之人的手，把他们从你们面前赶出，将他们的地赐给你们』；
verses.en: I rescued you from Egypt’s power[NOTE:1] and from the power of all who oppressed you. I drove them out before you and gave their land to you.
notes: Heb “hand” (also a second time later in this verse).
verses.commentary:
6:9 "dispossessed them" This VERB (BDB 176, KB 204, Piel IMPERFECT
with waw) is used several times to denote the Canaanites being driven out of the land.

- by divinely directed hornets, Exod. 23:28

- by divine empowering of Israel, Exod. 23:31; Jos. 24:12

- by YHWH Himself, Exod. 23:29, 30; 33:2 (by His angel); Deut. 33:27; Jos. 24:18; Jdgs. 2:3; 6:9

The conquest was an act of Israel's God, not her military! Canaan was YHWH's land.

▣ "gave you their land" YHWH gave Israel the land of Canaan. It is often said to be "His land." He
removed the native tribes because of their sin and idolatry (cf. Gen. 15:12-21).

When Israel sinned and committed idolatry, He removed them also (i.e., the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles).

verses.zh: 又对你们说：『我是耶和华―你们的　神。你们住在亚摩利人的地，不可敬畏他们的　神。你们竟不听从我的话。』」
verses.en: I said to you, “I am the Lord your God! Do not worship[NOTE:1] the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you are now living.” But you have disobeyed me.’”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Do not fear.”
Heb “you have not listened to my voice.”
verses.commentary:
6:10 "I am the Lord your God" This is covenant language using both YHWH and
Elohim (cf. Exod. 20:2; Deut. 5:2-3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY,
C. and D.

▣ "fear" See SPECIAL TOPIC:
FEAR (OT).

▣ "the Amorites" See
SPECIAL TOPIC:
PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE.

▣ "But you have not obeyed Me" The source of the problem was not God's impotence (cf. Jdgs. 6:13),
but Israel's lack of faith and obedience (cf. Jdgs. 2:2) to the covenant (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

▣ "Amorites" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: AMORITE.

verses.zh: 耶和华的使者到了俄弗拉，坐在亚比以谢族人约阿施的橡树下。约阿施的儿子基甸正在酒榨那里打麦子，为要防备米甸人。
verses.en: The angel of the Lord[NOTE:1] came and sat down under the oak tree in Ophrah owned by Joash the Abiezrite. He arrived while Joash’s son Gideon[NOTE:2] was threshing[NOTE:3] wheat in a winepress[NOTE:4] so he could hide it from the Midianites.[NOTE:5]
notes: The angel of the Lord is also mentioned in Judg 2:1.

Heb “Now Gideon his son….” The Hebrew circumstantial clause (note the pattern vav [ו] + subject + predicate) breaks the narrative sequence and indicates that the angel’s arrival coincided with Gideon’s threshing.
Heb “beating out.”

Threshing wheat in a winepress. One would normally thresh wheat at the threshing floor outside the city. Animals and a threshing sledge would be employed. Because of the Midianite threat, Gideon was forced to thresh with a stick in a winepress inside the city. For further discussion see O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 63.
Heb “Midian.”
verses.commentary:
6:11 "the angel of the Lord" When one compares Jdgs. 6:11 with 6:14, it seems
obvious that we are dealing here with another theophany, or possibly the pre-Incarnate Jesus Christ. Here, he is called "the
angel of the Lord," while in Jdgs. 6:20 he is called "the angel of God." We know that Gideon
believed him to be God because of 6:22, 23. He believed they were going to die (cf. Gen. 16:13; 32:30; Exod. 20:19; 33:20;
Num. 12:8; Jdgs. 13:21-23; Isa. 6:5) because they saw God, which they came to understand meant this angel was a
manifestation of Deity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANGEL OF THE Lord

▣ "and sat under the oak which was in Ophrah" Ophrah was very close to the destroyed city of Ai.
There is a possible connection between the oak at Ophrah and the oaks of Mamre during Abraham's life (cf. Gen. 18:1).
Trees were a common sacred site (cf. Gen. 12:6; 35:4, 8; Deut. 11:20; Jos. 19:33; 24:26; Jdgs. 4:5; 9:37; 1 Sam. 10:3;
31:13; 1 Chr. 10:12), probably because they reveal the presence of underground water.

▣ "the Abiezrite" Joshua 17:2 states that this was a clan of Manasseh (cf. 1 Chr. 7:18). They settled on
the western side of the Jordan.

▣ "Gideon was beating the grain in the wine press in order to save it from the Midianites" This shows
two things.

- Gideon was hiding his crop from the annual raid

- There was not a very large crop so that it could be thrashed in a wine press

verses.zh: 耶和华的使者向基甸显现，对他说：「大能的勇士啊，耶和华与你同在！」
verses.en: The angel of the Lord appeared and said to him, “The Lord is with you, courageous warrior!”
verses.commentary:
6:12 "The Lord is with you" Notice that Gideon changes this to "the
Lord is with us" in Jdgs. 6:13. At this point Gideon did not recognize this angel as
representing God. He even addresses the angel in a way that shows he is wondering where God is in his life and the
life of his people.

▣ "O valiant warrior" This is sarcasm that turns into a prophecy.

There is a possibility that this CONSTRUCT (BDB 150 plus 298) was a title for nobility
(cf. Ruth 2:1; 1 Sam. 9:1; 2 Kgs. 15:20; 1 Chr. 7:5; see NEB and REB's translations of Ruth 2:1).

verses.zh: 基甸说：「主啊，耶和华若与我们同在，我们何致遭遇这一切事呢？我们的列祖不是向我们说『耶和华领我们从埃及上来』吗？他那样奇妙的作为在哪里呢？现在他却丢弃我们，将我们交在米甸人手里。」
verses.en: Gideon said to him, “Pardon me,[NOTE:1] but if the Lord is with us, why has such disaster[NOTE:2] overtaken us? Where are all his miraculous deeds our ancestors told us about? They said,[NOTE:3] ‘Did the Lord not bring us up from Egypt?’ But now the Lord has abandoned us and handed us over to Midian.”
notes: Heb “But my lord.”
Heb “all this.”
Heb “saying.”
verses.commentary:
6:13 Gideon's question about YHWH's presence and deliverance in the past are addressed by the unnamed
prophet in Jdgs. 6:8. He is still God of Israel, delivering them for His purposes.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "lord" See full note online at Exod. 32:23.

▣ "But now the Lord has abandoned us" This is a powerful VERB
(BDB 643, KB 695, Qal PERFECT). Gideon and the Israelites felt that YHWH had abandoned them. They
did not fully realize the devastating consequences of covenant disobedience.

verses.zh: 耶和华观看基甸，说：「你靠着你这能力去从米甸人手里拯救以色列人，不是我差遣你去的吗？」
verses.en: Then the Lord himself[NOTE:1] turned to him and said, “You have the strength.[NOTE:2] Deliver Israel from the power of the Midianites![NOTE:3] Have I not sent you?”
notes: Some interpreters equate the Lord and the messenger in this story. Since the messenger represents the Lord, perhaps when the Lord is mentioned in vv. 14 and 16 it means so indirectly, while Gideon’s direct encounter is with the angel. Indicators that the Lord and the angel of the Lord are distinct include: 1) the Hebrew text says only “Lord” in vv. 14 and 16; 2) in verse 16 the speaker in the Hebrew text says “I will be with you” referring to the Lord (but see the note at v. 16); 3) Gideon addresses the angel as ‎אֲדֹנִי (ʾadoni, “my lord”) but the Lord as אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay, “my Lord”); 4) in vv. 22-23 the Lord and Gideon continue to carry on a conversation after the messenger has vanished (v. 21). On the other hand, if the Lord was present, appearing visibly in human form (called a theophany), as implied by “turning” [his head] to Gideon, why would Gideon not be more fearful at the end of the story for having seen God rather than his angel? The story could be pictured as an exchange with the angel followed by calling out to the Lord in prayer. The translation assumes that the angel and the Lord are distinct in the conversation, but the matter is difficult.tc The LXX reads “the angel of the Lord” here and in v. 16. The translation follows the MT and adds “himself” to draw attention to the change.
Heb “Go in this strength of yours.”
Heb “the hand of Midian.”
verses.commentary:
6:14 This is YHWH's mandate to Gideon. Notice that YHWH, here, "the angel of the Lord,"
turns and looks at Gideon. This is surely a theophany.

This is similar to God sending Moses in Exodus 3-4.

- YHWH uses human instrumentality

- YHWH's personal presence is the key to victory (Jdgs. 6:16)

- Gideon gives excuses, as Moses did, for not being able to fulfill YHWH's mandate (Jdgs. 6:15)

- he, like Moses, needs signs (cf. Jdgs. 6:17,37,39)

- but he is obedient (Jdgs. 6:25-27)

verses.zh: 基甸说：「主啊，我有何能拯救以色列人呢？我家在玛拿西支派中是至贫穷的。我在我父家是至微小的。」
verses.en: Gideon[NOTE:1] said to him, “But Lord,[NOTE:2] how[NOTE:3] can I deliver Israel? Just look! My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my family.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Gideon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Note the switch to אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay, “Lord”). Gideon seems aware that he is speaking to someone other than, and superior to, the messenger, whom he addressed as אֲדֹנִי (ʾadoni, “my lord”) in v. 13.
Heb “with what.”
Heb “in my father’s house.”
verses.commentary:
6:15 "How shall I deliver Israel" This sense of inadequacy is similar to that of Moses and Jeremiah. Notice Gideon
addresses the angel as "Lord" (Adon), not YHWH (Jdgs. 6:10). Gideon is not sure who this person is (cf. Jdgs. 6:22).

▣ "Behold, my family is the least in Manasseh" The Hebrew term (BDB 48), translated here "family," can also
mean the number "thousand." This is one of the problems in the OT; when to translate this term "thousand" or "family."

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

▣ "I am the youngest in my father's house" Normally the eldest son was responsible for doing great acts
for the family. Here is another example of God choosing, not only the least family in the tribe, but one other than the oldest
son. This is an OT way to assert the sovereignty of YHWH.

▣

NASB, NKJV, LXX, Peshitta
"my father's house"

JPSOA
"clan"

NRSV, TEV
"my family"

NJB, REB
"my father's family"

The term here is "אלפי"

(BDB 48, KB 60; NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 406-410) and denotes a "tribe" or "clan." The Hebrew root for "thousand" is very
similar (see NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 416-417 and chart at vol. 2, p. 1140).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND

verses.zh: 耶和华对他说：「我与你同在，你就必击打米甸人，如击打一人一样。」
verses.en: The Lord said to him, “Ah, but[NOTE:1] I will be with you! You will strike down the whole Midianite army.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “certainly.”
Heb “You will strike down Midian as one man.” The idiom “as one man” emphasizes the collective unity of a group (see Judg 20:8, 11). Here it may carry the force, “as if they were just one man.”
verses.commentary:
6:16 "surely I will be with you" This is the greatest promise that a human can receive—the promise of the
presence of God. This is a repeated promise: Gen. 26:3; 31:3; Exod. 3:12; Ps. 23:4; Matt. 28:20.

verses.zh: 基甸说：「我若在你眼前蒙恩，求你给我一个证据，使我知道与我说话的就是主。
verses.en: Gideon[NOTE:1] said to him, “If you really are pleased with me,[NOTE:2] then give me[NOTE:3] a sign as proof that it is really you speaking with me.
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Gideon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “If I have found favor in your eyes.”
Heb “perform for me.”
verses.commentary:
6:17 "If now I have found favor in Your sight, then show me a sign" This is the first indication of a weakness in
Gideon. It is an indicator of his lack of faith (cf. Jdgs. 6:36-40; 7:10). Gideon needed much physical encouragement from
YHWH. In this chapter alone, he requires three supernatural signs (i.e., Jdgs. 6:21, 37, 39). Be careful of signs (cf. Matt. 24:24).

verses.zh: 求你不要离开这里，等我归回将礼物带来供在你面前。」主说：「我必等你回来。」
verses.en: Do not leave this place until I come back[NOTE:1] with a gift[NOTE:2] and present it to you.” The Lord said, “I will stay here until you come back.”
notes: The Hebrew text adds “to you,” but this has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

Heb “and I will bring out my gift.” The precise nuance of the Hebrew word מִנְחָה (minkhah, “gift”) is uncertain in this context. It may refer to a gift offered as a sign of goodwill or submission. In some cases it is used of a gift offered to appease someone whom the offerer has offended. The word can also carry a sacrificial connotation.
verses.commentary:
6:18 "do not depart from here, until I come back" It took quite a long time to prepare this meal. This is
similar to Gen. 18:1-8. The angel remained because of the customs of that day.

verses.zh: 基甸去预备了一只山羊羔，用一伊法细面做了无酵饼，将肉放在筐内，把汤盛在壶中，带到橡树下，献在使者面前。
verses.en: Gideon went and prepared a young goat,[NOTE:1] along with unleavened bread made from an ephah of flour. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot. He brought the food[NOTE:2] to him under the oak tree and presented it to him.
notes: Heb “a kid from among the goats.”
The words “the food” are not in the Hebrew text (an implied direct object). They are supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
verses.commentary:
6:19 "an ephah of flour" This referred to a dry weight of between 35 and 45 pounds.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANCIENT NEAR EASTERN WEIGHTS AND VOLUMES

▣ "broth" This word (BDB 600) is used only twice.

- here as an offering to the angel of the Lord

- Isa. 65:4 in a negative sense of idolatry

It may be implied but not mentioned in Gen. 18:1-8; 19:3.

verses.zh: 神的使者吩咐基甸说：「将肉和无酵饼放在这磐石上，把汤倒出来。」他就这样行了。
verses.en: God’s angel said to him, “Put the meat and unleavened bread on this rock,[NOTE:1] and pour out the broth.” Gideon did as instructed.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Take the meat…and put [it] on this rock.”
Heb “and he did so.”
verses.commentary:
6:20 "Take the meat and the unleavened bread and lay them on this rock, and pour out the broth. And he did so" This
was a very significant sacrifice in light of the scarcity of food. This text has three IMPERATIVES.

verses.zh: 耶和华的使者伸出手内的杖，杖头挨了肉和无酵饼，就有火从磐石中出来，烧尽了肉和无酵饼。耶和华的使者也就不见了。
verses.en: The angel of the Lord touched the meat and the unleavened bread with the tip of his staff.[NOTE:1] Fire flared up from the rock and consumed the meat and unleavened bread. The angel of the Lord then disappeared.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “extended the tip of the staff which was in his hand and touched the meat and unleavened bread.”
Heb “went from his eyes.”
verses.commentary:
6:21 "the staff that was in his hand" YHWH appeared (i.e., theophany) in a way (i.e., dress and staff) as Gideon
would have expected.

Since there have been so many parallels with YHWH's initial call of Moses, possibly "the staff"
represented the power of YHWH, as Moses' staff did.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "and fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread" Again, God
was giving Gideon a sign so he would know that He was with him.

verses.zh: 基甸见他是耶和华的使者，就说：「哀哉！主耶和华啊，我不好了，因为我觌面看见耶和华的使者。」
verses.en: When Gideon realized[NOTE:1] that it was the angel of the Lord, he[NOTE:2] said, “Oh no![NOTE:3] Sovereign Lord![NOTE:4] I have seen the angel of the Lord face-to-face!”
notes: Heb “saw.”
Heb “Gideon.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Or “Ah!”
The Hebrew text reads אֲדֹנַי יְהוִה (ʾadonay yehvih, “Lord [the same title used in v. 15], Lord”).

verses.zh: 耶和华对他说：「你放心，不要惧怕，你必不致死。」
verses.en: The Lord said to him, “You are safe![NOTE:1] Do not be afraid. You are not going to die!”
notes: Heb “Peace to you.” For a similar use of this idiom to introduce a reassuring word, see Gen 43:23.
verses.commentary:
6:23 "The Lord said to him, 'Peace to you, do not fear; you shall not die'" These
were tremendous words of comfort (cf. Gen. 43:23) and also another sign to Gideon that God was with him. Kimchi, the
famous Jewish commentator, says that God was speaking from heaven (i.e., Bath kol) because the angel of the
Lord had departed (cf. Jdgs. 6:21).

verses.zh: 于是基甸在那里为耶和华筑了一座坛，起名叫「耶和华沙龙」（就是耶和华赐平安的意思）。（这坛在亚比以谢族的俄弗拉直到如今。）
verses.en: Gideon built an altar for the Lord there, and named it “The Lord is on friendly terms with me.”[NOTE:1] To this day it is still there in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
notes: Heb “The Lord is peace.” Gideon’s name for the altar plays on the Lord’s reassuring words to him, “Peace to you.”
verses.commentary:
6:24 "The Lord is Peace" This is a combination of YHWH and a
NOUN. This combination was common and formed many titles for YHWH.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPECIAL TOPIC: SHALOM (peace)

▣ "To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites" This is one of the many textual hints (i.e., like "unto
this day") that the book of Judges was compiled by a later editor.

verses.zh: 当那夜，耶和华吩咐基甸说：「你取你父亲的牛来，就是（或译：和）那七岁的第二只牛，并拆毁你父亲为巴力所筑的坛，砍下坛旁的木偶，
verses.en: That night the Lord said to him, “Take the bull from your father’s herd, as well as a second bull, one that is seven years old.[NOTE:1] Pull down your father’s Baal altar and cut down the nearby Asherah pole.
notes: Or “Take a bull from your father’s herd, the second one, the one seven years old.” Apparently Gideon would need the bulls to pull down the altar.
verses.commentary:
6:25 "Now on the same night" This implies a revelation during a dream. This was common in the OT.

▣ "Take your father's bull and a second bull seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal" This
seems to imply the use of a yoke of oxen. The age of the bull may link it to the time period that Israel had been
oppressed by Midian, which was seven years (cf. Jdgs. 6:1). It may also relate to seven being the perfect number
in the Bible.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE

▣ "pull down the altar of Baal" Before Gideon could deliver Israel he had to deliver his own family from
the idolatry that plagued his people. Ba'al was the male fertility god and Asherah was the female consort.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANCIENT NEAR EAST

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL'S MANDATED RESPONSE TO CANAANITE FERTILITY WORSHIP

verses.zh: 在这磐石（原文是保障）上整整齐齐地为耶和华―你的　神筑一座坛，将第二只牛献为燔祭，用你所砍下的木偶作柴。」
verses.en: Then build an altar for the Lord your God on the top of this stronghold according to the proper pattern.[NOTE:1] Take the second bull and offer it as a burnt sacrifice on the wood from the Asherah pole that you cut down.”
notes: Possibly “in a row” or “in a layer,” perhaps referring to the arrangement of the stones used in the altar’s construction.
verses.commentary:
6:26

NASB, NRSV, JPSOA
"stronghold"

NKJV, Peshitta
"rock"

TEV
"mound"

NJB
"strong-point"

REB
"earth-work"

LXX
"peak"

This term (BDB 732) has several connotations.

- natural stronghold

- mountain, cave, ravine ‒ Jdgs. 6:26

- harbor ‒ Isa. 23:4,11,14

- manmade strongholds ‒ Isa. 17:9; Ezek. 24:25

- a place of safety (i.e., YHWH) ‒ 2 Sam. 22:2,33; Ps. 27:1; 28:8

This raised earthen site already had a Ba'al altar, now it was the site of a new altar to YHWH.
The Ba'al altars were located on naturally occurring high places or were manmade dirt platforms, several feet
high.

verses.zh: 基甸就从他仆人中挑了十个人，照着耶和华吩咐他的行了。他因怕父家和本城的人，不敢在白昼行这事，就在夜间行了。
verses.en: So Gideon took 10 of his servants[NOTE:1] and did just as the Lord had told him. He was too afraid of his father’s family[NOTE:2] and the men of the city to do it in broad daylight, so he waited until nighttime.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “men from among his servants.”
Heb “house.”
Heb “so he did it at night.”
verses.commentary:
6:27 "Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the Lord had spoken to
him; and it came about, because he was too afraid of his father's household and the men of the city to do it by day,
that he did it by night" Here again is another symbol of Gideon's mixture of fear and doubt. He did what God said
but he did it by night so no one would know. You can't keep something secret very long when ten men were involved.
It also shows that this altar to Ba'al was a local shrine encompassing more than just the family of Gideon.

verses.zh: 城里的人清早起来，见巴力的坛拆毁，坛旁的木偶砍下，第二只牛献在新筑的坛上，
verses.en: When the men of the city got up the next morning, they saw[NOTE:1] the Baal altar pulled down, the nearby Asherah pole cut down, and the second bull sacrificed on the newly built altar.
notes: Heb “look!” The narrator uses this word to invite his audience/readers to view the scene through the eyes of the men.

verses.zh: 就彼此说：「这事是谁做的呢？」他们访查之后，就说：「这是约阿施的儿子基甸做的。」
verses.en: They said to one another,[NOTE:1] “Who did this?”[NOTE:2] They investigated the matter thoroughly[NOTE:3] and concluded[NOTE:4] that Gideon son of Joash had done it.
notes: Heb “each one to his neighbor.”
Heb “this thing.”
Heb “they inquired and searched.” The synonyms are joined to emphasize the care with which they conducted their inquiry.
Heb “and said.” Perhaps the plural subject is indefinite. If so, it could be translated, “they were told.”
verses.commentary:
6:29 "Joash" This name (BDB 219) is a combination of YHWH and "strong" or "given." His name shows the
amalgamation of Ba'al and Yahwehistic worship in this period. Gideon's acts show a Yahwehistic altar replacing a
Ba'al/Asherah altar.

verses.zh: 城里的人对约阿施说：「将你儿子交出来，好治死他；因为他拆毁了巴力的坛，砍下坛旁的木偶。」
verses.en: The men of the city said to Joash, “Bring out your son, so we can execute him![NOTE:1] He pulled down the Baal altar and cut down the nearby Asherah pole.”
notes: Heb “and let him die.” The jussive form with vav after the imperative is best translated as a purpose clause.
verses.commentary:
6:30 This verse has

- a Hiphil IMPERATIVE ‒ "bring out"

- a Qal JUSSIVE ‒ "that he may die"

verses.zh: 约阿施回答站着攻击他的众人说：「你们是为巴力争论吗？你们要救他吗？谁为他争论，趁早将谁治死！巴力若果是神，有人拆毁他的坛，让他为自己争论吧！」
verses.en: But Joash said to all those who confronted him,[NOTE:1] “Must you fight Baal’s battles?[NOTE:2] Must you rescue him? Whoever takes up his cause[NOTE:3] will die by morning![NOTE:4] If he really is a god, let him fight his own battles![NOTE:5] After all, it was his altar that was pulled down.”[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “to all who stood against him.”
Heb “Do you fight for Baal?”
Heb “fights for him.”

Whoever takes up his cause will die by morning. This may be a warning to the crowd that Joash intends to defend his son and to kill anyone who tries to execute Gideon. Then again, it may be a sarcastic statement about Baal’s apparent inability to defend his own honor. Anyone who takes up Baal’s cause may end up dead, perhaps by the same hand that pulled down the pagan god’s altar.
Heb “fight for himself.”
Heb “for he pulled down his altar.” The subject of the verb, if not Gideon, is indefinite (in which case a passive translation is permissible).
verses.commentary:
6:31 This shows the wisdom of Gideon's father (Joash, Jdgs. 6:29) as the men of the city reacted to the loss
of their local shrine. Gideon's father stood up for his son and said that if Ba'al be a god, let him contend for himself.

▣ "Whoever will plead for him shall be put to death by morning" This seems to be a threat by Joash
to protect his son.

verses.zh: 所以当日人称基甸为耶路・巴力，意思说：「他拆毁巴力的坛，让巴力与他争论。」
verses.en: That very day Gideon’s father named him Jerub Baal,[NOTE:1] because he had said, “Let Baal fight with him, for it was his altar that was pulled down.”
notes: Heb “He called him on that day Jerub Baal.” The name means, at least by popular etymology, “Let Baal fight” or “Let Baal defend himself.”
verses.commentary:
6:32 "Jerubbaal" Gideon's name was changed to "one who contends with Ba'al" (BDB 937), which is a
popular etymology but not the exact meaning of the name ("may Ba'al take action").

verses.zh: 那时，米甸人、亚玛力人，和东方人都聚集过河，在耶斯列平原安营。
verses.en: All the Midianites, Amalekites, and the people from the east[NOTE:1] assembled. They crossed the Jordan River[NOTE:2] and camped in the Jezreel Valley.
notes: Heb “Midian, Amalek, and the sons of the east.”
The words “the Jordan River” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarification.
verses.commentary:
6:33 "the valley of Jezreel" This is the same as the valley of Esdraelon or the plains of Megiddo, which
will later be called Armageddon. This shows how far north the coalition had penetrated (cf. Jdgs. 6:3).

verses.zh: 耶和华的灵降在基甸身上，他就吹角；亚比以谢族都聚集跟随他。
verses.en: The Lord’s Spirit took control of[NOTE:1] Gideon. He blew a trumpet,[NOTE:2] summoning the Abiezrites to follow him.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “clothed.”
That is, “mustered an army.”
Heb “Abiezer was summoned after him.”
verses.commentary:
6:34 "the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon" This literally means "the Spirit
of the Lord 'clothed' Gideon." What a beautiful metaphor of the power of the presence of
God. It occurs only three times in the OT (cf. 1 Chr. 12:18; 2 Chr. 24:20)

▣ "and he blew a trumpet" The blowing of the trumpet was a signal for the men to rally to war. The
acts of deliverance were not accomplished by human power, intellect, or numbers but by YHWH's Spirit. The way
it is described varies.

- "clothed" ‒ Jdgs. 6:34

- "came upon" ‒ Jdgs. 11:29

- "stir" (lit. "impel," BDB 821, KB 952, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) ‒ Jdgs. 11:29

- "rush upon" (BDB 852, KB 1026) ‒ Jdgs. 14:6,19; 15:14

Note the variety! The author is purposely using synonyms or quoting from oral or written sources.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

verses.zh: 他打发人走遍玛拿西地，玛拿西人也聚集跟随他；又打发人去见亚设人、西布伦人、拿弗他利人，他们也都出来与他们会合。
verses.en: He sent messengers throughout Manasseh and summoned them to follow him as well.[NOTE:1] He also sent messengers throughout Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they came up to meet him.
notes: Heb “and he also was summoned after him.”

verses.zh: 基甸对　神说：「你若果照着所说的话，藉我手拯救以色列人，
verses.en: Gideon said to God, “If you really intend to use me to deliver Israel,[NOTE:1] as you promised, then give me a sign as proof.[NOTE:2]
notes: More literally, “you are about to deliver Israel by my hand.”
The words “then give me a sign as proof” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

verses.zh: 我就把一团羊毛放在禾场上：若单是羊毛上有露水，别的地方都是干的，我就知道你必照着所说的话，藉我手拯救以色列人。」
verses.en: Look, I am putting a wool fleece on the threshing floor. If there is dew only on the fleece, and the ground around it[NOTE:1] is dry, then I will be sure[NOTE:2] that you will use me to deliver Israel,[NOTE:3] as you promised.”
notes: Heb “and on all the ground.”
Or “know.”
Heb “you will deliver Israel by my hand.”

verses.zh: 次日早晨基甸起来，见果然是这样；将羊毛挤一挤，从羊毛中拧出满盆的露水来。
verses.en: The Lord did as he asked.[NOTE:1] When he got up the next morning, he squeezed the fleece, and enough dew dripped from it to fill a bowl.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “And it was so.”
Heb “dew dripped from the fleece—a bowl full of water.”

verses.zh: 基甸又对　神说：「求你不要向我发怒，我再说这一次：让我将羊毛再试一次。但愿羊毛是干的，别的地方都有露水。」
verses.en: Gideon said to God, “Please do not get angry at me, when I ask for just one more sign.[NOTE:1] Please allow me one more test with the fleece. This time make only the fleece dry, while the ground around it is covered with dew.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Let your anger not rage at me, so that I might speak only this once.”
Heb “Let the fleece alone be dry, while dew is on all the ground.”
verses.commentary:
6:39 "Do not let Your anger burn against me" This is similar to Abraham's statement as he bargained with
God over Sodom and Gomorrah (cf. Gen. 18:22-33).

▣ "that I may speak once more" This is similar to Abraham's speaking to YHWH in Gen. 18:32.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own
interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation.
You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of
the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why are histories of Gideon and Samson given in so much detail?

- Who are "the sons of the east"?

- Why is the prophet unnamed in Jdgs. 6:8? Is he the only unnamed prophet in the OT?

- Who is "the angel of the Lord"?

- Why is Gideon called "O valiant warrior"?

- Why is Jdgs. 6:16 such a significant theological verse?

- Why is "a sign" of Jdgs. 6:17 a problem?

- Why did Gideon think he would die in Jdgs. 6:22?

- How did the worship of Ba'al reappear after Joshua's conquest?

- What does Jdgs. 6:34 imply? Is it unique in the OT?

verses.en: That night God did as he asked.[NOTE:1] Only the fleece was dry and the ground around it was covered with dew.
notes: Heb “God did so that night.”

BACKGROUND STUDY

- The account of Gideon goes from Judges 6:1 to 8:28. Samson and Gideon are dealt with in more detail than the other "judges."

- Gideon is a strange mixture of doubt and fear.

- This is the fifth cycle of apostasy and deliverance within the book of Judges.

- Many scholars see the combination of two accounts in Judges 6 (see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 306-307;
Jerome Biblical Commentary, p. 154).

- Judges 6:11-24

- Judges 6:25-32

I do not see the need for this. It simply follows the trend of J.E.P.D, which I reject. I much prefer this
oral history of John H. Walton and D. Brent Sandy, The Lost World of Scripture.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PENTATEUCH SOURCE CRITICISM (J,E,D,P)

- The famous account of Gideon putting out the fleece, found in Judges 6:36-40, is really an act of unbelief, not faith, and,
therefore, is not for us to emulate. The Bible records many things that it does not advocate.

- For the anthropomorphic language of this ancient account see Special Topic: The Problems and Limitations of Human
Language and Special Topic: Anthropomorphic Language to Describe God.
